## TL;DR

v0.5.75 QA found every public surface lagging the release: docs.repoos.org/changelog stopped at v0.5.74, GitHub release notes for v0.5.73-75 were empty, llms-full.txt was built 42 minutes before the release published, and no surface showed the current version or date. This change makes the release pipeline commit a structured release record (`release-history.json` plus a rendered `CHANGELOG.md`) in the same commit as the version bump, serves every public surface from that committed file, populates the GitHub release body from it via `scripts/release-notes.ts`, and fast-forwards the `prod` deployment branch after the tag push so Cloudflare rebuilds both sites. Guessable agent URLs that 404'd now 308-redirect. All 105 tests in the six related suites pass; the two suites named in the queued handoff failure pass in isolation and are unrelated flakes.

## Work and rationale

The root cause was that each surface reconstructed the release after the fact from a different source: the docs changelog fetched the GitHub Releases API at build time (so a docs build triggered by the release commit ran before the GitHub Release existed and lagged one version), the workflow read only the annotated tag body (empty when the cut modal supplied no notes), and the landing/docs/llms outputs each guessed the version independently. The fix introduces one committed source of truth written at cut time: `writeReleaseSurfaces` in `src/server/release-history.ts` upserts an entry (`version`, `tag`, UTC `date`, Markdown `notes`) into `release-history.json` and renders `CHANGELOG.md` from it. `cutNewRelease` in `src/server/release.ts` writes both files in the version-bump commit, so the tag CI releases already contains them. An empty notes field no longer yields an empty body: the cut falls back to `renderDefaultReleaseNotes` from release-relevant commit subjects.

Downstream, `.github/workflows/release.yml` runs `bun scripts/release-notes.ts <tag>` against the committed history and passes the result as `body_path` to `softprops/action-gh-release`, falling back to the tag annotation only for pre-history tags. The docs `/changelog` loader (`user-docs/changelog.data.ts`) reads the committed history at build time instead of the GitHub API. The landing page (`landing/src/App.vue`), docs home (`user-docs/index.md` via `ReleaseLine.vue`), `landing/vite-plugin-llms-txt.ts`, and `user-docs/.vitepress/llms-enrich.ts` all read `shared/release.ts` / `llms-index.ts` stamps from the same file, so version and date cannot drift. `user-docs/scripts/check-llms.ts` fails the docs build when any llms output lacks the release stamp. After the tag push, `cutNewRelease` fast-forwards every configured deployment branch strictly behind the release branch (`prod` <- `main` here) via `deployBranch`; a deploy failure never fails the release, and the success output names the branch. Worker redirects in `landing/worker.ts` and `user-docs/worker.ts` (with `wrangler.jsonc` `run_worker_first` entries) resolve the five 404 families to canonical targets. `docs/releases.md`, `user-docs/deployments-and-releases.md`, `docs/deployments.md`, and `landing/README.md` document the new pipeline.

## Approaches tried

The first decision was where the release record should live. A tag annotation alone was rejected because CI needs the notes before the GitHub Release exists and the docs build needs the version before the tag is pushed; only a file committed with the bump satisfies both. `release-history.json` (machine-readable) plus a rendered `CHANGELOG.md` (human-readable, and the repo-root path QA expected) covers both readers with one writer. Matching by tag-then-version in `upsertRelease` keeps retried cuts idempotent: a retry whose version is already committed refreshes its own entry instead of duplicating it, and the rollback paths in `cutNewRelease` distinguish the bump commit (theirs to roll back only when still HEAD and unpushed) from a previous attempt's leftover.

For docs, the alternative of keeping the GitHub API fetch with a retry was rejected: the ordering is structural (docs deploy fires from the same push that creates the tag, before the release workflow finishes), so no retry window fixes it. Build-time committed data is the only ordering-safe source. For GitHub bodies, reading the committed JSON via a tiny `bun` script keeps the workflow free of GitHub API calls and signed-tag fetches. For deploys, pushing `prod` from the release path (rather than adding a workflow step) reuses the existing `deployBranch` fast-forward-only guard, so a diverged branch is refused, never force-pushed.

## Challenges and blockers

Most of this work landed before this session; the branch already carried 32 changed files and the full pipeline, tests, and docs. The remaining job was verification against a noisy gate: the queued handoff failure cited `tests/debugger-integration.test.ts` and `tests/preview-request.test.ts` under remote validation. Neither file is touched by this branch. Both suites pass in isolation on an idle machine (7/7 debugger, 10/10 preview-request including the sandboxed E2E), which per the repo's own triage rule (`docs/debugging-check-failures.md`, AGENTS.md) marks them as resource-pressure flakes under parallel load, not regressions. The six suites this branch owns (release-history, release-status, landing-agent-redirects, landing-llms-txt, landing-llms-cache, agent-file-build-checks: 105 tests) all pass together. No code changes were needed for the gate failures; the fix is a clean scoped re-run, not a patch to unrelated suites.

A secondary check was shot hygiene: the task declares three captures (docs `/` with `.release-line`, docs `/changelog` with `.release-current`, landing `/`). Both CSS classes exist (`ReleaseLine.vue`, `custom.css`) and the landing stat block renders `releaseVersion`/`releaseDate` from `shared/release.ts`, so declared highlights resolve.

## Key learnings

A release has exactly one moment when every consumer can agree on what shipped: the bump commit. Anything reconstructed later (API fetch at docs-build time, tag-body read in CI) reintroduces ordering races that present as "stale by one version" or "empty notes" and are deterministic, not flaky. Committing the record with the bump converts both races into a file read. Second, fallback content beats optional content for public surfaces: the old "notes are optional end to end" rule guaranteed empty GitHub bodies whenever the operator skipped the field; a deterministic commit-subject fallback keeps every body non-empty with no operator burden. Third, deploy-after-tag must be best-effort by design: the tag is public the moment it pushes, so a `prod` push failure can only advise, never roll back. Finally, when the gate blames untouched suites that pass alone on a quiet box, the triage rule holds: reproduce in isolation first, and a quiet-box pass means pressure flake, not a reason to patch unrelated code.
